catalog_quote: The two main prosodic features in Agarabi are tone and nasalisation. Stress is predictable. There are two degrees of tone, high and low. These are primarily level tones though a slight glide on a phonetically short vowel may be perceived when there is a transition from one level to another in succeeding syllables. Otherwise, pitch glides occur only on phonetically long vowels and are interpreted as a sequence of low-high or high-low tones.[8]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Agarabi is described as a two-tone (high/low) language in which stress is non-contrastive ('predictable'). The source does not say where the predictable stress falls; no placement rule, no examples with stress marks, and no relation to tone is stated. Tone (acute = high) is the marked prosody in citation forms.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned for stress. For tone: pitch glides on short vowels are treated as transitions between levels; glides on long vowels as LH or HL sequences; fn. 8 notes tone perturbation across word boundaries is marked only inside phonetic brackets.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level description of prosodic features in a grammar sketch; examples are isolated words in phonetic brackets with tone marked by acute. Nasalisation is the other prosody and is discussed at length; stress gets the single sentence.
new_statements.identity_note: Goddard's data are from Punano village, Kainantu Sub-District, Eastern Highlands (Goddard 1967 introduction, fieldwork 1960-65); the SIL 2002 OPD calls the language 'Bare (Agarabi)' and the ANU recordings spell it 'Agarabe'. All refer to the same language-level languoid agar1252 (ISO agd); no dialect is singled out.

new_statements.quote: p. 100, sec. 4.2.4: "(Again the auxiliary carries the tense, aspect and person suffixes. There is also a tone change on the stem which is normally low tone.)" | p. 78, sec. 1: "If special emphasis is to be given to the fact that it took place a very long time ago the first syllable of peepah is drawn out and the tone change over the vowels is longer and higher than normal." | p. 79, sec. 2: "Sentences are usually characterised by falling intonation on the final verb and by pause."

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog classification tonal (Goddard 1980): the 1974 original treats Agarabi as having lexical tone (verb stems 'normally low tone', tone marks) but contains no phonology or prosody section and says nothing about word stress. The catalog's stress sentence ('Stress is predictable', 1980 PL A-56 sec. 1.2 p. 39) was added in the 1980 revision and has no 1974 counterpart, so the 1980 paper remains the only source for it; nothing here contradicts it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule or statement in this version. Tone: verb stems are normally low-toned and change tone under the contrary-to-fact auxiliary; high tone written with an acute accent in examples; tones not recorded for the long sample text. Only sentence-level intonation (falling on the final verb + pause; rising for exclamations/vocatives) is described.
new_statements.identity_note: Agarabi [agd], ca. 15,000 speakers around Kainantu, Eastern Highlands Province; Goddard's data from Punano village 1960-1974 (Goddard 1980 fn. 1). SIL records 23736 and 23657 list Subject Language Agarabi [agd]; the SIL OPD (Olson & Olson) calls the language Bare (Agarabi).

new_statements.quote: p. 72, Footnotes, fn. 1: "The Agarabi language has a two tone system; high tone is marked by an acute accent. I do not guarantee the accuracy of the notation as I do not hear tone accurately. For the same reason I have not taken into account any grammatical differences indicated by tonal changes." | p. 7, Symbolization: "v́ high tone¹ ( v = any vowel)" | p. 9, Introduction: "A terminal clause which has an independent (final) verb, falling intonation and is followed by pause is, then, interpreted as marking paragraph terminus."

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog classification tonal (Goddard 1980: two level tones): fn. 1 states 'a two tone system; high tone is marked by an acute accent'. Silent on word stress (a discourse-level study: sentence, paragraph, discourse); nothing bears on the 1980 'Stress is predictable' statement. Caveat: pp. 15-57 (sentence/paragraph types) were not read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress statement. Tone: two-tone system (high vs low), high tone written with an acute accent, author disclaims accuracy of tone notation and ignores grammatical tone alternations. Intonation is discussed only as a sentence/paragraph boundary signal (final verb + falling intonation + pause = paragraph terminus in her analysis).
new_statements.identity_note: Agarabi [agd], ca. 15,000 speakers around Kainantu, Eastern Highlands Province; Goddard's data from Punano village 1960-1974 (Goddard 1980 fn. 1). SIL records 23736 and 23657 list Subject Language Agarabi [agd]; the SIL OPD (Olson & Olson) calls the language Bare (Agarabi).
